records.source: וַיְהִ֣י רָעָב֩ בִּימֵ֨י דָוִ֜ד שָׁלֹ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֗ים שָׁנָה֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י שָׁנָ֔ה וַיְבַקֵּ֥שׁ דָּוִ֖ד אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑הסוַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־שָׁאוּל֙ וְאֶל־בֵּ֣ית הַדָּמִ֔ים עַל־אֲשֶׁר־הֵמִ֖ית אֶת־הַגִּבְעֹנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And was [a] famine in [the] days of David three years, year after year; and sought David [the] face of Yahweh. And said Yahweh, [It is] on Saul and on [the] house of the bloods, because he put to death the Gibeonites.
pieces: In the days of David there was a famine for three years in a row, so David sought the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, "It is because of Saul and his bloodstained house, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

L.1: And there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year; and David sought the face of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "[It is] because of Saul and because of [his] house of blood, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

R.1: While David was king, there was a famine that went on for three years, one year after another. So David went to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} why. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} answered, "It is because Saul and his family are guilty of shedding blood. Saul put the Gibeonites to death."

decisions.choice: in the days of David: at a time the text does not fix
alternatives: late in David's reign, after Absalom's revolt
decisions.reason: Chapters 21 to 24 gather accounts from different parts of David's reign, not in the order they happened. This one must come after chapter 9, since Mephibosheth son of Jonathan is already known to David (verse 7), but the text gives no closer date.

decisions.choice: a famine three years running: a sign that something was wrong between Israel and the LORD
decisions.reason: Drought and failed harvests were among the warnings the law gave for a people under the LORD's displeasure (Leviticus 26:19-20; Deuteronomy 28:23-24). A famine that did not lift after one bad year led David to ask the reason.

decisions.choice: sought the face of the LORD: came before the LORD to ask for an answer
decisions.reason: To seek someone's face is to seek their presence and favor (Psalm 27:8; Hosea 5:15). Here it brings an answer, so it includes asking the LORD what was wrong. The text does not say how the answer came; elsewhere David asks through a priest with the ephod (1 Samuel 23:9-12).

decisions.choice: the house of blood: a family that bears the guilt of blood unjustly shed
decisions.reason: The plural word "bloods" is used for blood shed by violence and the guilt it brings (Genesis 4:10; 2 Samuel 16:7-8). The guilt lies on Saul and on his household, the family line that ruled with him. Saul's killing of the Gibeonites is not told anywhere else.

decisions.choice: went to the LORD and asked him why; are guilty of shedding blood
decisions.reason: Readable says what seeking the LORD's face meant here, since an answer follows, and spells out "house of blood" as a family guilty of shedding blood.

records.heading: The Gibeonites are avenged

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֥א הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ לַגִּבְעֹנִ֖ים וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וְהַגִּבְעֹנִ֞ים לֹ֣א מִבְּנֵ֧י יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל הֵ֗מָּה כִּ֚י אִם־מִיֶּ֣תֶר הָאֱמֹרִ֔י וּבְנֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ נִשְׁבְּע֣וּ לָהֶ֔ם וַיְבַקֵּ֤שׁ שָׁאוּל֙ לְהַכֹּתָ֔ם בְּקַנֹּאת֥וֹ לִבְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה׃
records.gloss: And called the king to the Gibeonites and said to them; and the Gibeonites not from [the] sons of Israel [were] they, but rather from [the] remnant of the Amorite, and [the] sons of Israel had sworn to them; and sought Saul to strike them in his zeal for [the] sons of Israel and Judah.
pieces: So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (The Gibeonites were not {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}; they were what was left of the Amorites. The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} had sworn an oath to them, but in his zeal for the {{gender:people|sons}} of Israel and Judah, Saul had tried to wipe them out.)

L.2: And the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (Now the Gibeonites, they [were] not of the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites, and the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel had sworn to them; but Saul sought to strike them down in his zeal for the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel and Judah.)

R.2: The king called for the Gibeonites and talked with them. (The Gibeonites were not {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}. They were the last of the Amorites, one of the peoples who lived in the land before Israel came. The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} had sworn an oath to let them live. But Saul had tried to kill them all, because he was so eager to do what he thought was good for the {{gender:people|sons}} of Israel and Judah.)

decisions.choice: an aside about who the Gibeonites were
decisions.reason: After the king calls the Gibeonites, the narrator stops to explain who they were and why Saul's act was a crime. David's words follow in verse 3.

decisions.choice: the oath sworn to the Gibeonites in Joshua's day
decisions.reason: The Gibeonites tricked Israel into a treaty, and the leaders of Israel swore to them by the LORD to let them live (Joshua 9:3-27). Israel kept that oath even after the trick came to light, and the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the house of God. To kill them was to break an oath made in the LORD's name.

decisions.choice: the Amorites: a general name for the peoples of Canaan before Israel
decisions.reason: Joshua 9:7 and 11:19 call the people of Gibeon Hivites. Here "Amorites" is used in its wider sense for the earlier inhabitants of the land (Genesis 15:16; Joshua 24:15).

decisions.choice: in his zeal: Saul acted from a misplaced eagerness for his own people
decisions.reason: The text grants that Saul meant to serve Israel and Judah, but his zeal broke the oath Israel had sworn. Israel and Judah are named side by side, as they were in Saul's time (1 Samuel 11:8; 17:52).

decisions.choice: parentheses around the aside
decisions.reason: Every level sets the explanation in parentheses so the reader sees the story pause and resume in verse 3.

decisions.choice: one of the peoples who lived in the land before Israel came; sworn an oath to let them live; what he thought was good for
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the Amorites were, what the oath promised (Joshua 9:15) and that Saul's zeal was his own idea of Israel's good.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל־הַגִּבְעֹנִ֔ים מָ֥ה אֶעֱשֶׂ֖ה לָכֶ֑ם וּבַמָּ֣ה אֲכַפֵּ֔ר וּבָרְכ֖וּ אֶת־נַחֲלַ֥ת יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said David to the Gibeonites, What shall I do for you, and with what shall I make atonement, and bless [the] inheritance of Yahweh?
pieces: David asked the Gibeonites, "What should I do for you? How can I make atonement, so that you will bless the inheritance of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"

L.3: And David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you, and with what shall I make atonement, so that you bless the inheritance of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"

R.3: David asked the Gibeonites, "What can I do for you? How can I make atonement for this wrong, so that you will bless the people who belong to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"

decisions.choice: make atonement: put right the wrong so that its guilt is removed
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for atonement at the altar, but here no sacrifice is in view. David asks what will cover the wrong done to the Gibeonites, so that the blood guilt no longer rests on the land (Numbers 35:33).

decisions.choice: and bless: the purpose of the atonement, so that you will bless
alternatives: a separate request: and then bless
decisions.reason: The command "bless" follows the question and gives its aim. The wronged Gibeonites would no longer call for justice against Israel, but speak a blessing over it.

decisions.choice: the inheritance of the LORD: Israel, the people and land that belong to him
decisions.reason: Israel is called the LORD's inheritance, his own possession (1 Samuel 10:1; 26:19; 2 Samuel 20:19).

decisions.choice: make atonement
decisions.reason: As set for these books, the verb is "make atonement" at every level, so the reader can see it is the same word as in the law. Readable adds "for this wrong" and says "the people who belong to the LORD" for "the inheritance of the LORD".

records.source: וַיֹּ֧אמְרוּ ל֣וֹ הַגִּבְעֹנִ֗ים אֵֽין־לָ֜נוּ כֶּ֤סֶף וְזָהָב֙ עִם־שָׁא֣וּל וְעִם־בֵּית֔וֹ וְאֵֽין־לָ֥נוּ אִ֖ישׁ לְהָמִ֣ית בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מָֽה־אַתֶּ֥ם אֹמְרִ֖ים אֶעֱשֶׂ֥ה לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And said to him the Gibeonites, Not to us [is] silver or gold with Saul and with his house, and not to us [is] a man to put to death in Israel. And he said, What [are] you saying I shall do for you?
pieces: The Gibeonites answered him, "Our claim against Saul and his family is not a matter of silver or gold, and it is not our right to put anyone in Israel to death." David said, "Then what are you asking me to do for you?"

L.4: And the Gibeonites said to him, "[It is] not silver or gold [between] us and Saul and his house, and [it is] not for us to put any man to death in Israel." And he said, "What [are] you saying I should do for you?"

R.4: The Gibeonites answered, "We do not want silver or gold from Saul or his family. And we have no right to put anyone in Israel to death." David asked, "Then what do you want me to do for you?"

decisions.choice: silver or gold: a payment instead of a life
decisions.reason: The Gibeonites refuse to settle the matter with money. The law did not allow a payment to stand in place of the life of someone guilty of murder, because blood shed in the land could be atoned for only by the blood of the one who shed it (Numbers 35:31-33).

decisions.choice: not for us to put anyone to death: we have no right to take vengeance ourselves
alternatives: we do not wish anyone in Israel killed
decisions.reason: As people living under Israel's protection, the Gibeonites could not put an Israelite to death on their own authority. The words also hint at what they want: a death sentence that only the king could allow.

decisions.choice: David's words are a question: what do you say I should do?
alternatives: a promise: whatever you say, I will do for you
decisions.reason: The words can be read as a promise or as a question. Read as a question, David presses them to name what they want, and they do so in verses 5-6. Either way David is ready to act.

decisions.choice: Our claim ... is not a matter of silver or gold (Balanced); We do not want silver or gold (Readable)
alternatives: We have no silver or gold with Saul
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "there is not to us silver or gold with Saul" means their dispute with Saul's house is not about money. Balanced and Readable say that plainly. Both name David as the speaker of the last words.

records.source: וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר כִּלָּ֔נוּ וַאֲשֶׁ֖ר דִּמָּה־לָ֑נוּ נִשְׁמַ֕דְנוּ מֵֽהִתְיַצֵּ֖ב בְּכָל־גְּבֻ֥ל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And they said to the king, The man who consumed us and who planned against us, we have been destroyed from standing in all [the] territory of Israel,
pieces: They said to the king, "As for the man who nearly wiped us out and plotted against us, so that we have no place left anywhere in the territory of Israel,

L.5: And they said to the king, "The man who consumed us and who plotted against us, so that we have been destroyed from having a place in all the territory of Israel,

R.5: They told the king, "Saul nearly wiped us out. He made plans to destroy us so that none of us would be left anywhere in Israel's land.

decisions.choice: the man who ...: the sentence names Saul first and goes on in verse 6
decisions.reason: The speakers begin with "the man who consumed us" and break off, and the sentence resumes in verse 6 with what they ask for from his sons. The broken grammar fits people speaking with strong feeling.

decisions.choice: consumed us: brought us near to an end
decisions.reason: The verb means to finish or make an end of. Since Gibeonites are still alive, it describes how close Saul came to destroying them, or what he set out to do.

decisions.choice: destroyed from standing in all the territory of Israel: left with no place anywhere in the land
alternatives: so that we should be destroyed and have no place
decisions.reason: To "stand" in a land is to have a place and a right to live in it. The perfect verb "we have been destroyed" may state the result of Saul's plan or what he meant to achieve.

decisions.choice: Saul nearly wiped us out.
decisions.reason: Readable names Saul and turns the broken sentence into whole sentences.

records.source: יֻתַּן־לָ֜נוּ שִׁבְעָ֤ה אֲנָשִׁים֙ מִבָּנָ֔יו וְהוֹקַֽעֲנוּם֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה בְּגִבְעַ֥ת שָׁא֖וּל בְּחִ֣יר יְהוָ֑הסוַיֹּ֥אמֶר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲנִ֥י אֶתֵּֽן׃
records.gloss: let be given to us seven men from his sons, and we will impale them to Yahweh in Gibeah of Saul, [the] chosen of Yahweh. And said the king, I will give.
pieces: let seven of his male descendants be handed over to us, and we will impale them before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Gibeah of Saul, the one {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} chose." The king said, "I will hand them over."

L.6: let seven men from his sons be given to us, and we will impale them to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And the king said, "I will give [them]."

R.6: Hand over to us seven of Saul's sons and grandsons. We will put them to death and hang their bodies on poles before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Gibeah, Saul's hometown. Saul was the king {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} chose." The king said, "I will hand them over to you."

decisions.choice: impale: put to death and display the bodies
decisions.reason: This is the rare verb of Numbers 25:4 (see the note there). It describes a public execution with the bodies left on display; the exact method is not certain.

decisions.choice: his sons: his male descendants
decisions.reason: "Sons" includes grandsons. Verse 8 names two of Saul's sons and five of his grandsons.

decisions.choice: to the LORD: the act is done before the LORD to remove the guilt from the land
decisions.reason: Blood shed in the land, and an oath sworn in the LORD's name and broken, were matters between Israel and the LORD (Numbers 35:33; Joshua 9:19-20). The Gibeonites ask that the guilt be dealt with before him.

decisions.choice: at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD
alternatives: at Gibeon, on the mountain of the LORD
decisions.reason: The traditional Hebrew text, followed here, names Saul's hometown Gibeah (1 Samuel 10:26; 11:4) and calls Saul "the chosen of the LORD", recalling 1 Samuel 10:24. The ancient Greek translation reads differently, and some think the original said "at Gibeon, on the mountain of the LORD", which would match "on the mountain before the LORD" in verse 9. If the Hebrew is right, the title is a bitter reminder of the king the LORD had chosen.

decisions.choice: male descendants (Balanced); sons and grandsons; put them to death and hang their bodies on poles; Saul's hometown (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that grandsons are included (verse 8). Readable spells out the execution as in Numbers 25:4 and says what Gibeah was to Saul.

records.source: וַיַּחְמֹ֣ל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עַל־מְפִי־בֹ֖שֶׁת בֶּן־יְהוֹנָתָ֣ן בֶּן־שָׁא֑וּל עַל־שְׁבֻעַ֤ת יְהוָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בֵּֽינֹתָ֔ם בֵּ֣ין דָּוִ֔ד וּבֵ֖ין יְהוֹנָתָ֥ן בֶּן־שָׁאֽוּל׃
records.gloss: And spared the king Mephibosheth son of Jonathan son of Saul, because of [the] oath of Yahweh that [was] between them, between David and between Jonathan son of Saul.
pieces: But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that bound David and Saul's son Jonathan to each other.

L.7: And the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the oath of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that [was] between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.

R.7: But the king did not hand over Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul. David and Jonathan had made a promise to each other in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and David kept it.

decisions.choice: the oath between David and Jonathan
decisions.reason: Jonathan made David swear never to cut off his faithful love from Jonathan's house, and they swore to each other in the LORD's name for their descendants (1 Samuel 20:14-17, 42). David had already kept that promise by taking Mephibosheth into his household (chapter 9).

decisions.choice: the oath of the LORD: an oath sworn in the LORD's name, with him as witness
decisions.reason: Breaking Israel's oath to the Gibeonites caused this crisis; David now keeps his own oath sworn by the same LORD.

decisions.choice: spared: had pity on, and so did not give up
decisions.reason: The verb means to feel pity and so hold back from harming or giving someone up (1 Samuel 15:3, 9).

decisions.choice: did not hand over; and David kept it
decisions.reason: Readable says what sparing meant here and makes clear that David acted to keep his promise.

records.source: וַיִּקַּ֣ח הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ אֶת־שְׁ֠נֵי בְּנֵ֨י רִצְפָּ֤ה בַת־אַיָּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָלְדָ֣ה לְשָׁא֔וּל אֶת־אַרְמֹנִ֖י וְאֶת־מְפִבֹ֑שֶׁת וְאֶת־חֲמֵ֗שֶׁת בְּנֵי֙ מִיכַ֣ל בַּת־שָׁא֔וּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָלְדָ֛ה לְעַדְרִיאֵ֥ל בֶּן־בַּרְזִלַּ֖י הַמְּחֹלָתִֽי׃
records.gloss: And took the king [the] two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and [the] five sons of Michal daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.
pieces: Instead the king took the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, together with the five sons Saul's daughter Michal had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai of Meholah.

L.8: And the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

R.8: The king took the two sons Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, had had with Saul. Their names were Armoni and Mephibosheth. He also took the five sons Saul's daughter Michal had had with Adriel son of Barzillai, from the town of Meholah.

decisions.choice: Michal
decisions.reason: The traditional Hebrew text, followed here, reads Michal. But it was Saul's older daughter Merab who was given to Adriel the Meholathite (1 Samuel 18:19), and Michal had no child to the day of her death (6:23). A few Hebrew manuscripts and some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation read Merab, which may well be original. An old Jewish explanation keeps Michal by saying that she raised her sister's sons.

decisions.choice: this Mephibosheth is Saul's son by Rizpah, not Jonathan's son
decisions.reason: Two men in Saul's family bore the name. The one spared in verse 7 is Jonathan's son; this one is Saul's own son by his concubine Rizpah (3:7).

decisions.choice: the Meholathite: from Meholah, probably Abel-meholah
decisions.reason: As in 1 Samuel 18:19. This Barzillai is not the Gileadite who helped David in 17:27.

decisions.choice: of Meholah (Balanced); from the town of Meholah (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1 Samuel 18:19, Balanced and Readable say where Adriel came from.

records.source: וַֽיִּתְּנֵ֞ם בְּיַ֣ד הַגִּבְעֹנִ֗ים וַיֹּקִיעֻ֤ם בָּהָר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיִּפְּל֥וּ שְׁבַעְתָּ֖ם יָ֑חַד וְהֵ֨מָּה הֻמְת֜וּ בִּימֵ֤י קָצִיר֙ בָּרִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ים בִּתְחִלַּ֖תקְצִ֥יר שְׂעֹרִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he gave them into [the] hand of the Gibeonites, and they impaled them on the mountain before Yahweh, and fell [the] seven of them together; and they were put to death in [the] days of harvest, in the first [days], at [the] beginning of [the] harvest of barley.
pieces: He handed them over to the Gibeonites, who impaled them on the mountain before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. All seven of them died together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

L.9: And he gave them into the hand of the Gibeonites, and they impaled them on the mountain before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the seven of them fell together. And they were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first [days], at the beginning of the barley harvest.

R.9: He handed them over to the Gibeonites. They put all seven to death together and hung their bodies on poles on the hill before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. This happened in the first days of the harvest, when people were starting to cut the barley.

decisions.choice: impaled: put to death and displayed
decisions.reason: As in verse 6.

decisions.choice: fell together: died together
decisions.reason: To "fall" is often to die, especially by violence (1 Samuel 31:8; 2 Samuel 1:19).

decisions.choice: the beginning of the barley harvest: in early spring
decisions.reason: Barley was the first grain to ripen, around April (Ruth 1:22). After three years of famine, this was the season when the land's harvest was at stake.

decisions.choice: the seven of them; and they; at the beginning
decisions.reason: In three places the letters written in the text differ slightly from the way the text is traditionally read. The reading tradition is followed here; the differences do not change the sense.

decisions.choice: put all seven to death ... and hung their bodies on poles; on the hill
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the execution as in verse 6, and says "hill" for the high ground where it took place.

records.source: וַתִּקַּ֣ח רִצְפָּה֩ בַת־אַיָּ֨ה אֶת־הַשַּׂ֜ק וַתַּטֵּ֨הוּ לָ֤הּ אֶל־הַצּוּר֙ מִתְּחִלַּ֣ת קָצִ֔יר עַ֛ד נִתַּךְ־מַ֥יִם עֲלֵיהֶ֖ם מִן־הַשָּׁמָ֑יִם וְלֹֽא־נָתְנָה֩ ע֨וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֜יִם לָנ֤וּחַ עֲלֵיהֶם֙ יוֹמָ֔ם וְאֶת־חַיַּ֥ת הַשָּׂדֶ֖ה לָֽיְלָה׃
records.gloss: And took Rizpah daughter of Aiah the sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from [the] beginning of harvest until was poured water on them from the heavens; and not she allowed [the] birds of the heavens to rest on them by day, or [the] beasts of the field by night.
pieces: Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and laid it out on the rock as a place for herself. From the beginning of the harvest until rain fell on the bodies from the sky, she did not let the birds come down on them by day or the wild animals by night.

L.10: And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water poured on them from the heavens; and she did not let the birds of the heavens settle on them by day, or the beasts of the field by night.

R.10: Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, took some sackcloth, the rough cloth people wore to show their grief, and spread it out on the rock as a place to stay. She stayed there from the beginning of the harvest until the rain came and fell on the bodies. In the daytime she kept the birds away from them, and at night she kept the wild animals away.

decisions.choice: sackcloth spread on the rock: a mourner's place to sit and lie
decisions.reason: Sackcloth was coarse cloth worn in grief (3:31; Genesis 37:34). Rizpah spread it on the rock where the bodies were and made it her resting place for the whole of her watch.

decisions.choice: until water poured on them from the heavens: until the rain came
alternatives: an unexpected rain soon after the harvest began
decisions.reason: In Israel the rains normally return in the autumn, about six months after the barley harvest, so Rizpah may have kept watch for months. Rain at harvest time was rare (1 Samuel 12:17-18), so an early rain could also be meant, a sign that the drought and famine were ending. The text does not say which.

decisions.choice: keeping off the birds and animals: guarding the dead from the worst disgrace
decisions.reason: To be left as food for birds and wild animals was the most shameful end a person could suffer (Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Samuel 17:44, 46). Rizpah could not stop the execution, but she would not let the bodies be torn apart.

decisions.choice: rain; the birds; the wild animals
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the plain words for these fixed phrases. Readable explains what sackcloth was and why she spread it.

records.source: וַיֻּגַּ֖ד לְדָוִ֑ד אֵ֧ת אֲשֶׁר־עָשְׂתָ֛ה רִצְפָּ֥ה בַת־אַיָּ֖ה פִּלֶ֥גֶשׁ שָׁאֽוּל׃
records.gloss: And it was told to David what had done Rizpah daughter of Aiah, [the] concubine of Saul.
pieces: Word reached David of what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done.

L.11: And it was told to David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.

R.11: Someone told David what Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, had done. She had been Saul's concubine (a secondary wife).

decisions.choice: concubine: a wife of lower rank
decisions.reason: As in 3:7, where Rizpah was the cause of the quarrel between Ish-bosheth and Abner. Her loyalty to Saul's sons moves David to act for the whole of Saul's house.

decisions.choice: concubine (a secondary wife)
decisions.reason: As set for these books, Readable explains "concubine" the first time it appears in a chapter.

records.source: וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ דָּוִ֗ד וַיִּקַּ֞ח אֶת־עַצְמ֤וֹת שָׁאוּל֙ וְאֶת־עַצְמוֹת֙ יְהוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנ֔וֹ מֵאֵ֕ת בַּעֲלֵ֖י יָבֵ֣ישׁ גִּלְעָ֑ד אֲשֶׁר֩ גָּנְב֨וּ אֹתָ֜ם מֵרְחֹ֣ב בֵּֽית־שַׁ֗ן אֲשֶׁ֨ר תְּלָא֥וּם שָׁ֨מָּה֙ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים בְּי֨וֹם הַכּ֧וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֛ים אֶת־שָׁא֖וּל בַּגִּלְבֹּֽעַ׃
records.gloss: And went David and took [the] bones of Saul and [the] bones of Jonathan his son from [the] lords of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from [the] square of Beth-shan, where had hung them the Philistines on [the] day [the] Philistines struck down Saul on Gilboa.
pieces: David went and took the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from the leading men of Jabesh-gilead. They had carried them off secretly from the open square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them up on the day they struck Saul down on Gilboa.

L.12: And David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the lords of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them on the day the Philistines struck down Saul on Gilboa.

R.12: Then David went to the leaders of Jabesh-gilead and got from them the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan. Those men had secretly taken the bodies from the town square in Beth-shan. The Philistines had hung them there on the day they killed Saul on Mount Gilboa.

decisions.choice: the men of Jabesh-gilead and the bodies of Saul and his sons
decisions.reason: After the battle on Mount Gilboa the Philistines hung the bodies of Saul and his sons on the wall of Beth-shan, and the brave men of Jabesh-gilead took them down by night and buried their bones at Jabesh (1 Samuel 31:8-13). David had blessed them for it (2:4-7).

decisions.choice: lords: the leading citizens of the town
decisions.reason: The word means owners or masters, and with a town's name it means its free, landholding citizens, who made decisions for it (Judges 9:2-3; 1 Samuel 23:11-12).

decisions.choice: stolen them from the square: took them away in secret from the open space by the gate
decisions.reason: "Stolen" here means taken without the Philistines' knowledge, not a wrong. 1 Samuel 31:10 says the bodies were fastened to the wall; the town square lay inside the gate, next to the wall.

decisions.choice: leading men (Balanced); leaders (Readable); carried them off secretly
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid "lords" and "stolen", which would suggest rulers and a crime. Readable adds "Mount" to Gilboa as in 1 Samuel 31:1.

records.source: וַיַּ֤עַל מִשָּׁם֙ אֶת־עַצְמ֣וֹת שָׁא֔וּל וְאֶת־עַצְמ֖וֹת יְהוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנ֑וֹ וַיַּ֣אַסְפ֔וּ אֶת־עַצְמ֖וֹת הַמּוּקָעִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he brought up from there [the] bones of Saul and [the] bones of Jonathan his son; and they gathered [the] bones of the impaled [ones].
pieces: He brought up from there the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan, and the bones of the men who had been impaled were gathered too.

L.13: And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son; and they gathered the bones of those who had been impaled.

R.13: He brought the bones of Saul and Jonathan back from Jabesh. The bones of the seven men who had been put to death and hung on poles were also gathered.

decisions.choice: they gathered the bones of the impaled: the seven men of verse 9
decisions.reason: "They" are not named; it means that David's people gathered what remained of the seven men, so that they could be buried with Saul and Jonathan.

decisions.choice: bones: by now only bones remained
decisions.reason: Saul's and Jonathan's bodies had been burned and the bones buried at Jabesh years before (1 Samuel 31:12-13). The seven had been left exposed through Rizpah's long watch (verse 10).

decisions.choice: were gathered too (Balanced); were also gathered (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a passive for the unnamed "they". Readable names Jabesh, says "seven men" and explains "impaled" as in verse 6.

records.source: וַיִּקְבְּר֣וּ אֶת־עַצְמוֹת־שָׁא֣וּל וִיהוֹנָֽתָן־בְּ֠נוֹ בְּאֶ֨רֶץ בִּנְיָמִ֜ן בְּצֵלָ֗ע בְּקֶ֨בֶר֙ קִ֣ישׁ אָבִ֔יו וַֽיַּעֲשׂ֔וּ כֹּ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֖ה הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיֵּעָתֵ֧ר אֱלֹהִ֛ים לָאָ֖רֶץ אַֽחֲרֵי־כֵֽן׃פ
records.gloss: And they buried [the] bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in [the] land of Benjamin in Zela, in [the] tomb of Kish his father; and they did all that commanded the king. And was entreated God for the land after this.
pieces: They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father, at Zela in the territory of Benjamin. They did everything the king commanded, and after that God answered prayer for the land.

L.14: And they buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin, in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father; and they did all that the king commanded. And God was moved by prayer for the land after that.

R.14: They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the family tomb of Saul's father Kish, at Zela in the land of the tribe of Benjamin. They did everything the king ordered. After that, God answered their prayers for the land, and the famine came to an end.

decisions.choice: the tomb of Kish: Saul is laid with his ancestors
decisions.reason: To be buried in the family grave was an honor, and to lie outside it a disgrace (1 Kings 13:22). David gives Saul and Jonathan a proper burial in Saul's home territory of Benjamin. Zela was one of the towns of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28).

decisions.choice: the bones of Saul and Jonathan: the seven are not named
alternatives: adds: and the bones of those who had been impaled
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation adds that the bones of the seven were buried with them. The Hebrew text, followed here, does not say so, though verse 13 implies it by having their bones gathered.

decisions.choice: God was entreated for the land: God listened to prayer for the land and lifted the famine
decisions.reason: The verb means to let oneself be moved by prayer. The same words close the book in 24:25. The famine ended only after the guilt was dealt with and Saul's house given honorable burial.

decisions.choice: and the famine came to an end
decisions.reason: Readable says what God's answer meant, since the chapter began with the famine (verse 1).

records.source: וַתְּהִי־ע֧וֹד מִלְחָמָ֛ה לַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֵּ֨רֶד דָּוִ֜ד וַעֲבָדָ֥יו עִמּ֛וֹ וַיִּלָּחֲמ֥וּ אֶת־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים וַיָּ֥עַף דָּוִֽד׃
records.gloss: And was again war to [the] Philistines with Israel; and went down David and his servants with him, and they fought with [the] Philistines; and was weary David.
pieces: Once again there was war between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his men, and they fought against the Philistines, and David grew exhausted.

L.15: And there was war again between the Philistines and Israel. And David went down, and his servants with him, and they fought with the Philistines; and David grew weary.

R.15: Once more the Philistines were at war with Israel. David went down with his soldiers to fight them, and he became very tired.

decisions.choice: again there was war: one of several battles, not dated
decisions.reason: Verses 15-22 tell of four Philistine champions killed in different battles of David's reign. They are not in time order with the chapters before; David's wars with the Philistines are also told in 5:17-25 and 8:1. 1 Chronicles 20:4-8 tells the last three of these battles.

decisions.choice: his servants: his fighting men
decisions.reason: The king's servants here are the soldiers who go to war with him (11:1).

decisions.choice: David grew weary: the king was no longer young
decisions.reason: The note sets up the danger of the next verse and explains his men's oath in verse 17.

decisions.choice: men (Balanced); soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "servants". Balanced and Readable say "men" and "soldiers", since these are fighting men, not court officials.

records.heading: Battles with the Philistines

records.source: וְיִשְׁבִּ֨י בְּנֹ֜ב אֲשֶׁ֣ר׀בִּילִידֵ֣י הָרָפָ֗ה וּמִשְׁקַ֤ל קֵינוֹ֙ שְׁלֹ֤שׁ מֵאוֹת֙ מִשְׁקַ֣ל נְחֹ֔שֶׁת וְה֖וּא חָג֣וּר חֲדָשָׁ֑ה וַיֹּ֖אמֶר לְהַכּ֥וֹת אֶת־דָּוִֽד׃
records.gloss: And Ishbi-benob, who [was] among [the] descendants of the Rapha, and [the] weight of his spear [was] three hundred [shekels] weight of bronze, and he [was] girded [with] new, and he said to strike down David.
pieces: Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed {{units:about 7 1/2 pounds|300 shekels}}, and who was armed with a new weapon, meant to kill David.

L.16: And Ishbi-benob, who [was] among the descendants of the Rapha, the weight of whose spear [was] 300 [shekels] of bronze in weight, and [who was] girded [with something] new, thought to strike David down.

R.16: Ishbi-benob was one of the descendants of the giants called the Rapha. His bronze spear weighed {{units:about 7 1/2 pounds|300 shekels}}, and he was armed with a new weapon. He planned to kill David.

decisions.choice: Ishbi-benob, a name
decisions.reason: The letters written in the text could be read "and they stayed at Nob"; the reading tradition, followed here, gives the name Ishbi-benob. The name is not found anywhere else.

decisions.choice: the Rapha: the ancestor or people from whom these giants came
alternatives: a warrior band devoted to a god named Rapha
decisions.reason: "The Rapha" is linked with the Rephaim, an ancient people remembered for their great size (Deuteronomy 2:11, 20; 3:11). It may be the name of an ancestor or a name for the whole people; some take it as the name of a band of warriors. Verses 20 and 22 show that these men were remembered as giants of Gath.

decisions.choice: 300 shekels of bronze: about 7 1/2 pounds
decisions.reason: The unit is not named, but weights of this kind are counted in shekels (1 Samuel 17:5, 7). The word for spear occurs only here. Goliath's spearhead weighed twice as much (1 Samuel 17:7).

decisions.choice: girded with new: a new weapon or new armor; the noun is not given
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only that he was girded with something "new". A sword or belt was what a man girded on (20:8; 1 Samuel 17:39; 25:13).

decisions.choice: he said to strike down David: he meant to kill David
decisions.reason: "Said" here means "thought" or "intended" (Exodus 2:14; 2 Samuel 5:6).

decisions.choice: about 7 1/2 pounds, with 300 shekels as the alternative
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight, with the shekels as the setting. Literal keeps the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: a new weapon
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply a general word for what was missing (m4). Readable says who the Rapha were.

records.source: וַיַּֽעֲזָר־לוֹ֙ אֲבִישַׁ֣י בֶּן־צְרוּיָ֔ה וַיַּ֥ךְ אֶת־הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֖י וַיְמִיתֵ֑הוּ אָ֣ז נִשְׁבְּעוּ֩ אַנְשֵׁי־דָוִ֨ד ל֜וֹ לֵאמֹ֗ר לֹא־תֵצֵ֨א ע֤וֹד אִתָּ֨נוּ֙ לַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְלֹ֥א תְכַבֶּ֖ה אֶת־נֵ֥ר יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: And helped him Abishai son of Zeruiah, and he struck the Philistine and killed him. Then swore [the] men of David to him, saying, Not shall you go out again with us to the battle, and not shall you quench [the] lamp of Israel.
pieces: But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's help. He struck down the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men took an oath before him: "Never again will you go out with us to battle. You must not let the lamp of Israel be put out."

L.17: But Abishai the son of Zeruiah helped him, and he struck the Philistine and killed him. Then the men of David swore to him, saying, "You shall not go out again with us to battle, and you shall not put out the lamp of Israel."

R.17: But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to help David. He attacked the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men made a solemn promise to him. "You will never go out to battle with us again!" they said. "If you are killed, it will be as if the lamp that gives light to Israel has gone out."

decisions.choice: Abishai son of Zeruiah: David's nephew and Joab's brother
decisions.reason: Zeruiah was David's sister (1 Chronicles 2:16). Abishai was one of David's boldest fighters (1 Samuel 26:6-9; 2 Samuel 23:18).

decisions.choice: swore to him: his men bound themselves by oath
decisions.reason: The men are the subject of "swore". They took a solemn oath before the king that he would no longer go into battle with them.

decisions.choice: the lamp of Israel: David as the one in whom Israel's life and hope go on
decisions.reason: A lamp burning in a house was a sign of life in it, and the LORD's promise of a "lamp" for David meant that his line would go on (1 Kings 11:36; 15:4; Psalm 132:17). If David died, Israel's light would go out.

decisions.choice: and you shall not quench: so that you do not quench
decisions.reason: The second clause gives the reason for the first: David must stay away from battle so that Israel does not lose him.

decisions.choice: If you are killed, it will be as if the lamp that gives light to Israel has gone out.
alternatives: you shall not put out the lamp of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (m3) and the reason for the oath.

records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ אַֽחֲרֵי־כֵ֔ן וַתְּהִי־ע֧וֹד הַמִּלְחָמָ֛ה בְּג֖וֹב עִם־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים אָ֣ז הִכָּ֗ה סִבְּכַי֙ הַחֻ֣שָׁתִ֔י אֶת־סַ֕ף אֲשֶׁ֖ר בִּילִדֵ֥י הָרָפָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And it was after this, and was again the battle at Gob with [the] Philistines; then struck down Sibbecai the Hushathite Saph, who [was] among [the] descendants of the Rapha.
pieces: After this there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. That was when Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of the Rapha.

L.18: And it happened after this that there was again battle at Gob with the Philistines. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who [was] among the descendants of the Rapha.

R.18: Later there was another battle with the Philistines at a place called Gob. In that battle Sibbecai from Hushah killed Saph, another descendant of the giants called the Rapha.

decisions.choice: 1 Chronicles 20:4 tells this battle with small differences
decisions.reason: Chronicles places the battle at Gezer and spells the giant's name Sippai. Gob is not mentioned outside this chapter, so its place is not known.

decisions.choice: Sibbecai the Hushathite: one of David's warriors
decisions.reason: He is listed among David's mighty men and was later commander of the army division for the eighth month (1 Chronicles 11:29; 27:11). Hushah was a clan or town of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:4).

decisions.choice: the Rapha
decisions.reason: As in verse 16.

decisions.choice: Sibbecai from Hushah; a place called Gob
decisions.reason: Readable says where Sibbecai came from and marks Gob as a place name.

records.source: וַתְּהִי־ע֧וֹד הַמִּלְחָמָ֛ה בְּג֖וֹב עִם־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּ֡ךְ אֶלְחָנָן֩ בֶּן־יַעְרֵ֨יאֹרְגִ֜ים בֵּ֣ית הַלַּחְמִ֗י אֵ֚ת גָּלְיָ֣ת הַגִּתִּ֔י וְעֵ֣ץ חֲנִית֔וֹ כִּמְנ֖וֹר אֹרְגִֽים׃ס
records.gloss: And was again the battle at Gob with [the] Philistines; and struck down Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite Goliath the Gittite, and [the] wood of his spear [was] like a beam of weavers.
pieces: There was another battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, from Bethlehem, killed Goliath of Gath, whose spear had a shaft like a weaver's beam.

L.19: And there was again battle at Gob with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, and the shaft of his spear [was] like a weavers' beam.

R.19: There was yet another battle with the Philistines at Gob. In it Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, from Bethlehem, killed Goliath from Gath. The pole of Goliath's spear was like the heavy beam of a weaver's loom.

decisions.choice: Elhanan ... struck down Goliath the Gittite
alternatives: Elhanan ... struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text of Samuel, followed here, says that Elhanan killed Goliath of Gath. 1 Samuel 17 tells how David killed Goliath, and 1 Chronicles 20:5 says that Elhanan killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath. Several explanations are offered. Written in the original letters, the words "Lahmi the brother of" look much like "the Bethlehemite", so one account may have been miscopied from the other, and Chronicles may keep the original. Or the Chronicler may have made clear what Samuel left unsaid. Or a second champion of Gath bore the name Goliath. An old Jewish tradition took Elhanan to be another name for David. The text does not settle the question, and none of these is certain.

decisions.choice: Jaare-oregim: probably miscopied from the word "weavers" at the end of the verse
decisions.reason: The second part of the name, "oregim", is the word for "weavers" that closes the verse, and may have been copied into the name by mistake. Chronicles calls Elhanan's father Jair. The name is given here as the text has it.

decisions.choice: the shaft like a weavers' beam: the same description as 1 Samuel 17:7
decisions.reason: The spear is described in the words used for Goliath's spear in David's fight with him (see the note on 1 Samuel 17:7).

decisions.choice: from Bethlehem; of Gath (Balanced); from Gath (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the towns instead of using the forms "Bethlehemite" and "Gittite". Readable describes the spear in the words of 1 Samuel 17:7.

records.source: וַתְּהִי־ע֥וֹד מִלְחָמָ֖ה בְּגַ֑ת וַיְהִ֣י׀אִ֣ישׁ מָד֗וֹן וְאֶצְבְּעֹ֣ת יָדָיו֩ וְאֶצְבְּעֹ֨ת רַגְלָ֜יו שֵׁ֣שׁ וָשֵׁ֗שׁ עֶשְׂרִ֤ים וְאַרְבַּע֙ מִסְפָּ֔ר וְגַם־ה֖וּא יֻלַּ֥ד לְהָרָפָֽה׃
records.gloss: And was again battle at Gath, and was a man of stature, and [the] fingers of his hands and [the] toes of his feet [were] six and six, twenty and four in number; and also he was born to the Rapha.
pieces: There was another battle at Gath, where there was a man of great size who had six fingers on each of his hands and six toes on each of his feet, twenty-four altogether. He also was descended from the Rapha.

L.20: And there was again battle at Gath, and there was a man of great size, and the fingers of his hands and the toes of his feet [were] six and six, twenty-four in number; and he also was born to the Rapha.

R.20: Another battle took place at Gath. A very tall man was there who had six fingers on each of his hands and six toes on each of his feet, twenty-four altogether. He was another descendant of the giants called the Rapha.

decisions.choice: a man of great size
alternatives: a man of strife, a quarrelsome man
decisions.reason: The letters written in the text could be read as "Midian", and the reading tradition gives a word that usually means "strife". The parallel in 1 Chronicles 20:6 has "a man of stature", a giant, and the following clause and verse 22 support that sense here.

decisions.choice: six fingers and six toes: an extra finger on each hand and an extra toe on each foot
decisions.reason: Extra fingers and toes are a known condition that runs in families. It is noted here as a mark of this unusual family of warriors.

decisions.choice: born to the Rapha: descended from the Rapha
decisions.reason: As in verse 16.

decisions.choice: six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out "six and six" so the total of twenty-four is clear.

records.source: וַיְחָרֵ֖ף אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיַּכֵּ֨הוּ֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן בֶּן־שִׁמְעָ֖ה אֲחִ֥י דָוִֽד׃
records.gloss: And he taunted Israel, and struck him down Jonathan son of Shimeah [the] brother of David.
pieces: When he taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimeah, David's brother, killed him.

L.21: And he taunted Israel, and Jonathan the son of Shimeah, David's brother, struck him down.

R.21: This man mocked Israel's army, and Jonathan killed him. Jonathan was the son of David's brother Shimeah.

decisions.choice: taunted Israel: as Goliath had done
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of Goliath's challenge to the armies of Israel (1 Samuel 17:10, 25-26, 36).

decisions.choice: Shimeah
decisions.reason: The letters written in the text spell Shimei; the reading tradition, followed here, gives Shimeah. He is David's brother, called Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9 and Shimea in 1 Chronicles 2:13, and the father of Jonadab (13:3).

decisions.choice: David's brother: Shimeah, not Jonathan
decisions.reason: The phrase describes Shimeah, so Jonathan was David's nephew (1 Chronicles 2:13; 20:7).

decisions.choice: Israel's army
decisions.reason: Readable says that the taunt was aimed at Israel's fighting men, as in 1 Samuel 17:10.

records.source: אֶת־אַרְבַּ֥עַת אֵ֛לֶּה יֻלְּד֥וּ לְהָרָפָ֖ה בְּגַ֑ת וַיִּפְּל֥וּ בְיַד־דָּוִ֖ד וּבְיַ֥ד עֲבָדָֽיו׃פ
records.gloss: These four were born to the Rapha in Gath, and they fell by [the] hand of David and by [the] hand of his servants.
pieces: These four were descendants of the Rapha in Gath, and they fell at the hands of David and his men.

L.22: These four were born to the Rapha in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.

R.22: These four men were descendants of the giants of Gath called the Rapha. They died at the hands of David and his soldiers.

decisions.choice: these four: Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath and the man with six fingers
decisions.reason: The verse sums up verses 16-21, as 1 Chronicles 20:8 does for its three.

decisions.choice: by the hand of David and of his servants: in David's wars, by David's men
decisions.reason: None of the four was killed by David himself in these verses; his men struck the blows. As king, David shares the credit for victories won in his service.

decisions.choice: men (Balanced); soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.
